title: Developer Trust & Unit-Economics Positioning Compact
one_liner: Make LLM features predictable and cost-effective for engineering teams by turning performance and reliability into developer-first primitives.
body:
Purpose and audience:
This compact is a concise internal narrative for field teams and product marketers to explain why engineering and platform teams should choose Redwood. Target audience: engineering leads building product features, platform teams responsible for internal ML services, and ML/infra buyers evaluating tradeoffs between managed APIs and DIY inference.

Core mission framing (short):
We enable engineering teams to ship LLM-powered experiences where performance, cost, and reliability are predictable primitives — not variable outcomes.

Thesis (how we think about the market):
1) Competitive advantage has shifted from model ownership to the ability to operationalize models. Teams that win make inference repeatable, debuggable, and economical.
2) Developers adopt tools that minimize blast radius: simple rollback, predictable tail latency, and clear unit economics.
3) Product velocity comes from stable inference behavior — consistent latency, deterministic failovers, and transparent cost signals.

Why this positioning matters (problem statement):
- Today many teams face inconsistent tail latency, noisy cost per token, and brittle rollout practices across regions and models.
- Tooling gaps force engineering teams to choose between expensive dedicated infra or fragile self-hosting.
- Sales cycles for platform teams stall on vague promises about “scaling GPU clusters” — buyers want predictable SLOs and measurable unit economics before committing.

Redwood promise (how we translate thesis into a customer-facing idea):
- We turn inference into an engineering primitive: predictable latency SLOs, transparent per-call cost, and built-in fallbacks that keep products live.
- We provide the same operational surface across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments so teams can prototype quickly and graduate without rework.

Elevator pitch (30–45s):
For engineering teams building LLM features, Redwood is the inference platform that makes model-serving predictable and economical. Unlike one-off hosting or generic cloud endpoints, Redwood combines a high-throughput runtime, smart routing, and cost-aware controls so you can ship features fast without surprise costs or downtime.

Three messaging pillars (core claims + quick evidence hooks):
1) Predictable performance for product UX
   - Claim: Tail-latency SLOs and per-route tuning so user-facing features behave consistently.
   - Proof hooks: benchmarking dashboards, latency SLA language, customer case study showing stable 95th pct latency under burst.

2) Deterministic economics and observability
   - Claim: Transparent token economics, token-level cost breakdowns, and tooling that recommends batching/quantization changes with projected $/month impact.
   - Proof hooks: cost-simulation screenshots, Optimizer suggestions, API that returns cost estimates for a request.

3) Safe operationalization and migration paths
   - Claim: Canary rollouts, automatic fallback to compact variants, and same API surface across deployment modes so migrations are predictable.
   - Proof hooks: rollout UI, documented migration checklist, sample config for canary -> global rollout.

Positioning differentiators (practical language sales can use):
- Not just faster: we break down why it’s safe to route production traffic to LLMs — with fallbacks, observability, and cost-prescriptive ops.
- Not just cheaper: we make cost visible and actionable for engineers, aligning incentives between product and infra teams.
- Not just consistent: we give a migration path from prototype to compliant private deployment without API changes.

Competitor snapshot (talk tracks for objections):
- Generic cloud-managed endpoints: good for raw capacity but lack model-aware routing, KV/prefix caching, and engineered fallbacks. Rebuttal: Redwood supplies model variants and routing policies tailored to maintain UX under degraded conditions.
- DIY self-hosted runtimes: full control but long lead time, no standard observability, and high ops burden. Rebuttal: Redwood offers comparable runtime optimizations + operational guardrails and predictable unit economics.
- LLM API vendors focused on features: fast iteration but unpredictable costs and limited deployment isolation. Rebuttal: Redwood provides the same developer ergonomics with cost transparency and dedicated/private options.

Key proof points and data to prioritize in collateral:
- Quantified improvement: median token cost reduction or latency reduction for typical chat/QA workload after adopting Redwood Optimize suggestions.
- Case study: platform team that migrated an internal assistant from DIY infra to Redwood Dedicated and reduced operational incidents by X% while cutting effective $/100k queries by Y%.
- Architecture diagram: how requests route across tiers and how fallback policies work (visual).

Core positioning dos and don'ts (copy guidance):
- DO emphasize predictable outcomes and concrete metrics (SLOs, $/token, 95th pct latency).
- DO use engineering-first language (canary, KV cache, quantization profile) when speaking to builders.
- DO mention deployment parity: same API across hosted/dedicated/private.
- DON'T overpromise instant cost savings; frame Optimize as recommendation-driven with measurable gains over time.
- DON'T lean into model-ownership arguments — customers care more about serving.

Open questions and R&D hooks (things to validate with Eng/Product):
- What exact metric set will we publish as the ‘predictable outcome’ benchmark? (candidate: 95th pct latency, P50 cost per token, percent of calls served from cache)
- Can we produce a short reproducible benchmark that buyers can run against their sample prompt to see projected costs?
- How granular should the Optimize recommendations be for buyer-facing collateral? (e.g., per-model vs per-route recommendations)

Suggested collateral for immediate execution (first wave):
- A 1-page cheat sheet: "How Redwood makes inference predictable" with the three pillars and a micro-case study.
- Sales playbook one-pager: objection handling for platform teams and CFO questions about unit economics.
- Technical checklist for solutions engineers: migration steps, common pitfalls, and rollout templates.

Tone and stylistic guidance for customer-facing versions:
- Keep language concrete, metric-focused, and engineer-respectful. Avoid marketing hyperbole.
- Use short bulleted claims with clear proof hooks that link to data or demos.

Quick internal checklist to finalize this brief:
- [ ] Lock the benchmark metrics with Eng (owner: Ethan)
- [ ] Produce a reproducible cost/latency snippet for marketing site (owner: Product-Marketing)
- [ ] Draft the cheat-sheet for sales, iterate with Solutions Eng (owner: María)

Notes to self / rough copy artifacts to preserve:
- Several customer conversations flagged latency spikes during scale tests — we should capture one anonymized example for field materials.
- Solutions Eng asked for a migration runbook template (add to linked artifacts).

Bottom line (short):
Redwood reduces the uncertainty of building on LLMs by making performance and cost predictable, observable, and actionable — so engineering teams can ship features with the confidence they already expect from other core infra components.

- Any objections from Sales about the proposed rebuttals?
- Does this narrative align with the Dedicated pricing changes planned for H1?
